speechtext: Mr. MAXIME RAYMOND (Beauharnois-Laprairie) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 31, to amend the Companies Act, 1934.

subtopic: CONTROL OF PROFITS AND DIVIDENDS OF PROTECTED INDUSTRIES-OBLIGATIONS TO EMPLOYEES AND PUBLIC
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: CONTROL OF PROFITS AND DIVIDENDS OF PROTECTED INDUSTRIES-OBLIGATIONS TO EMPLOYEES AND PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year the royal commission appointed to investigate the textile industry in Canada made its report, which was tabled in the house during the session. The report shows that textile manufacturers, while continually complaining of insufficient tariff protection, have for a number of years enjoyed the advantage of customs duties. This tariff protection is a privilege secured by them from parliament upon representations that their workers would benefit by increased employment and better wages. Unfortunately, the facts revealed at the inquiry show that these companies, far from fulfilling the obligations entailed in the privileges granted to them, have taken advantage of these privileges to make exorbitant profits and distribute scandalous dividends and bonuses to their shareholders, while paying workers less than living wages. The object of this bill is to put an end to such abuses and to come to the aid of the worker, by enabling the Secretary of State to obtain information regarding the operations and management of industrial enterprises enjoying tariff protection, and to exercise some control over their profits and their dividend payments; in brief, to see that they carry out their obligations towards their employees and the public.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time. BANK ACT

Perhaps I should add that not only were the periods shortened under this agreement but the amount by which the valuation may be advanced was at the same time reduced. I take a memorandum prepared by the Canadian Horticultural Council as my basis for giving four examples to show how the progressive lessening of tariff protection for vegetables has worked out during three periods in the last few years. First of all I take the period under the Bennett administration; secondly the period under the 1935 agreement; and thirdly, the period under this last agreement which has been entered into. These, however, must be regarded as maximum total duties which only exist for a short period each year. For the balance of the year only the general tariff protection remains.
In the Dunning budget of 1930 the plight of the vegetable growers was recognized and a general tariff protection of thirty per cent was provided, but that was not regarded as sufficient at the time and in addition to the thirty per cent the then Minister of 
Finance (Mr. Dunning) applied for the first time minimum seasonal duties on imports into Canada. Up to the 1935 agreement the minimum seasonal tariff remained, and was supplemented by Mr. Bennett's advanced valuations in order to give further protection; but in 1936 the policy of progressive lessening in protection commenced. Let us see what has happened in the meantime to suggest to the government that we should have less protection for this kind of farm produce.

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
Since 1930 many conditions have changed, but all the conditions that have changed would call for a tightening and a raising of the tariff rather than a lessening of it. There developed in the meantime a much improved system of refrigerator transportation, which permits of fruits and vegetables from the United States arriving here in almost as good condition as when they left the field. In addition there has been an increase of nearly forty-five per cent in the production of fresh vegetables in the United States, and at the same time a reduction in the unit value of such commodities in the domestic market there. We must also take into consideration the numerous bonuses and subsidies given by the United States government on these and other farm products. Added to all these changed conditions, in the last eight years there has been a most comprehensive program of advertising of American fresh fruits and vegetables, not only in the United States but extending over here also.
The vegetable growing industry in Canada to-day is in a most vulnerable position, perhaps the most vulnerable that it has ever occupied. I need only point out one thing by way of evidence-I do not want to overstate the case, and of course if I do there are those who will pass judgment upon it. In a press release of November 21, 1938, by the executive of the Ontario Vegetable Growers' Association, meeting in Toronto, they said:
The trade agreement, with its serious reductions in both tariff and seasonal protection, will make it impossible to produce vegetables in Ontario on a commercial basis.
In the county I represent, in addition to the other types of vegetables, we grow potatoes. It is well therefore to make mention of the position of that branch of agriculture under this new agreement.
Before the agreement went into effect Canada imposed a tariff of 75 cents a hundredweight against United States potatoes the year round. Under this agreement potatoes come in from August 1 to June 14, ten and a half months of the year, free, and for the rest of the year the duty is cut in half. But the concessions by the United States to our potato growers are not so sweeping. Prior to this agreement our duty and theirs were the same, namely, 75 cents a hundredweight. If there is any branch of agriculture that is in real need of adequate statistics at present, it is the vegetable growing industry. By treatment similar to that given to the vegetable growers in Canada, the fruit grower has also suffered. But we went further than that, because this agreement was linked up with the agreement between the United Kingdom and the United States. Under the empire trade agreements the apple grower in Canada obtained a sheltered market in the United Kingdom, to the extent, using our own currency, of about $1.08 a hundredweight. That is, the United States grower in shipping his apples into the United Kingdom market had to jump a hurdle of $1.08 before he could compete on equal terms with the apple grower in Canada. Following that change there was a great revival of business among the apple growers of Canada. It put a great many of them on their feet. But under this new agreement the protection in that sheltered market has been cut from SI .08 to 72 cents a hundredweight.
I am not able to agree on all points with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley), although I know that in many matters his judgment is good. But the fruit growers I represent are not quite so complacently satisfied with the terms of the agreement as those in the minister's constituency are said to be. I can only suppose that his engaging personality and convincing power of argument must have been in evidence to induce his growers to take that view. In any event most of our people feel that this reduction to 72 cents is sufficient to allow the United States apple grower to jump the fence and compete with us in England.
I have nothing further to say in that regard, except to make one plea on behalf of the fruit and vegetable men at this time: that with all these changes in protective tariffs something will have to be done internally for this branch of agriculture. I say that most seriously. In the meantime, until we have an opportunity to restore some of these tariffs, I suggest that we do as they did in Ontario some years ago, namely, launch, with some kind of government assistance, in cooperation with the growers themselves, an "eat home grown fruit and vegetables" campaign among the housewives of Canada. I am sure the housewife is not always aware of the fact that when she buys carrots from the States while our products are available, she is interfering with the livelihood of some who are her Canadian friends in the vegetable and fruit growing districts. We should advertise and popularize our home grown fruit and vegetable products, because for deliciousness and

flavour there is nothing to equal them on the other side of the line or anywhere else in the world.
I want to give this instance, in closing. One of my friends in the county of Peel wanted to exchange a box of apples which he had grown for a crate of oranges which a friend of his had grown in the state of Florida. When he went to ship the box of apples, he found that it cost him $4.14 to ship it to Homestead, Florida. When the man in Florida shipped .the oranges back in the same box it cost only $3 to land that box in the county of Peel. I made inquiries and I received this explanation from the Canadian National Railways: You can ship a crate of oranges from Florida to Toronto for somewhere around $3, but this is due entirely to the fact that the United States has a special rate in effect from Florida to Canada to encourage the shipment of Florida oranges. In other words, it is just another subsidy.
I draw that to the attention of the house for the purpose of showing that we as Canadians must wake up. If we are going to protect our own growers we must do something other than lessen tariff protection while providing nothing in compensation by way of subsidization or organized assistance. That in short, Mr. Speaker, is the case of the fruit and vegetable growers in Canada, and I cannot over-emphasize the probable effect of these new arrangements upon that industry and those engaged in it.
In conclusion may I repeat that Canadians should await the practical results of this new agreement before rising to the heights of hilarity over its advantages. Common sense, if nothing else, dictates this course. Our job in this house is to legislate towards a better and a more prosperous Canada. In pointing out some of the obvious weaknesses in this pact we as members of his majesty's loyal opposition have, according to the best British parliamentary traditions, discharged our obligation to the people of the dominion. The final responsibility rests with the government.

Mr. Speaker, the trade treaty with the United States means a great deal to the province of New Brunswick, as well, of course, as to the other provinces of this dominion.
New Brunswick is one province which was not entirely carried away by the 1911 loyalty cry, because it returned in the election of that year a majority of supporters of the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Expressions of regret have been heard ever since that many were influenced by the political issue then made of loyalty to the British empire, because after the election it was clearly realized that

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
it was only a political cry, and that the reciprocity proposals, had they not been defeated by that cry, would have been of great economic benefit to the maritime provinces.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion), speaking in the house on Friday on this trade agreement, made certain statements about the 1935 general election returns, rather implying that the Liberal government elected was not representative of the people. But an examination of the 1935 election returns, by constituencies, shows that there were elected, by clear majorities of the votes cast, 90 Liberals and only 5 Conservatives; 9 Social Credit, one Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and one independent Conservative. Thus there were more than five times as many Liberals elected by clear majority votes than all the other parties put together, indicating that the Liberal government does well represent the voters.
The geographical situation of New Brunswick makes it a great convenience to trade with the United States, and the present trade treaty by which the United States gives reductions on potatoes, lumber, horses, cattle, maple products, blueberries and furs is a decided benefit and will result in very greatly increased trade during this year.
Reading the address of the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) I note that he states, at page 345 of Hansard:
It is generally realized that in New Brunswick conditions were never worse than they are at the present time.
And referring to the 1935 treaty with the United States he makes this statement, at page 344 of Hansard:
The right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said in effect that the people of Canada were blessed by the results of the 1935 treaty.
Again, on page 344, he says:
I simply want to say that as far as the primary producers of the maritime provinces are concerned, the statement made by the Prime Minister is not borne out by the facts.
But the hon. member has not given the facts. He refers to apples and states that the province of New Brunswick shipped about 48,523 barrels in 1936 to British empire markets, and that the 1937 shipments totalled 25,744 barrels. Having some knowledge of apple production in New Brunswick I noted at once that these figures were evidently about twenty-five times overstated and therefore entirely misleading.

I shall be glad to give the house the correct apple crop figures as supplied by the New Brunswick department of agriculture, and prepared under the direction of the provincial horticulturist.
As a matter of fact, 1936 was a poor apple production year for New Brunswick, there being only 29,104 barrels marketed, and of these, 20,147 ban-els were sold within the province and 8,957 outside, mostly in Quebec province. So it is very wrong to give the idea that there were 48,523 barrels sold from New Brunswick in British empire markets in 1936. The correct figures for 1937 are as follows: The crop increased to 49,616 barrels, of which 14,548 barrels were sold outside the province, again largely in Quebec province. It will thus be seen that the.facts are very different from what the hon. member purported to show. New Brunswick does not export apples to any great extent. Potatoes are New Brunswick's great export crop; Nova Scotia exports large quantities of apples.
While I have great personal esteem for the hon. member for Royal I have wondered why he should give figures which are at least twenty-five times overstated. Evidently it was done for political motives, due to the statement which had been made that the hon. member is equal to twenty-five other men. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) visited New Brunswick, and in paying tribute to the hon. member for Royal he said, as reported in the press of June 6, 1938, that the hon. member for Royal was equal to all the twenty-five members from the maritime provinces who were seated on the government side of the house. The further statement was made that he had been the only hon. member to stand up for New Brunswick. Of course this is political stuff, and no doubt it secured some votes for the hon. member for Greenwood at the Ottawa Conservative convention. It is unfortunate however to have the hon. member for Royal seeing figures twenty-five times their actual size.
While potatoes are the chief crop in New Brunswick, and while we do not export many apples, yet that portion of the St. John river valley in New Brunswick is highly suited to apple raising, and as a result the number of orchards is increasing. Mr. Speaker, I am rising to support the treaty. I believe treaties of this description are to be welcomed at the present time because they tend to bring about better international relations. I do not believe, as is so often contended in the house, that they offer any immediate relief to the domestic problems that confront this nation. Our immediate problems are of such a nature that international treaties of this type will not cure the ills from which the country suffers. Nevertheless I believe they are to be supported because they tend to improve the relationships between ourselves and other countries which are parties to these treaties.
Unfortunately national self-sufficiency is becoming more pronounced all across the world. Recent events in Europe show that the totalitarian states with that kind of philosophy are gaining great strength. Their domination of eastern and southern Europe in my opinion means still further restrictions in world trade. When he discussed the treaty in the house recently the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made the statement that he hoped the treaty would make for peace. I think perhaps he drew an over
[Mr. W. G. Clark.)
optimistic picture of what might be done in that regard. All I can say, as I said at the outset, is that I am supporting the treaty because I hope that something of that nature may in part at least be achieved. One thing the treaty does is this: it draws into closer cooperation the three great English-speaking democracies. When I speak of the three democracies I am thinking of the United States, Great Britain herself, and the democracies which comprise the British dominions. Those three divisions are drawn more closely together by an agreement of this description, and I believe that that is all to the good.
Moreover may I point out that closely associated with Great Britain to-day in the struggle for the preservation of democratic institutions is the old republic of France. Anything which can tend to bring these peoples more closely together at the present time may have the effect of preventing the outbreak of a serious and disastrous war. While the treaty is only a step in that direction I believe we ought to support it for this reason, if on no other grounds.
I do not propose to analyse at length the various proposals in the treaty. This has been done in the house quite extensively during the last few days. I think that almost everything that could be said pro and con about the treaty's definite proposals has been said already. However, there are other factors to which, particularly as one representing a western constituency, I should like to direct some attention.
First of all, in the consummation of this treaty once again the west was called upon to relinquish something which seemed at least to have superficial advantage. I know it has been argued that little advantage was derived from the wheat preference, but I contend it did give us some advantage. As I said

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
during a previous debate, I happened to be in the United States of America when the treaty was signed. I noticed that the middle western American newspapers were very much pleased with having at last got rid of the six cent preference. If, with the limited market we now have, that tends to encourage the use of more United States wheat by British mills, then it will have some effect upon our market. The point of view that I am expressing is not only the point of view of a member associated with this particular group; I submit it is also the point of view of many Liberals in western Canada. Gregory, the Liberal member for The Battlefords. I may be wrong, but I believe Mr. Gregory is the deputy speaker. This report reads:
Ringing challenge for a return to that sturdy Liberalism upon which the party was founded and strong denunciation of many eastern Liberals as merely adjuncts of the privileged classes of eastern industrialists was sounded in the legislature Tuesday by J. A. Gregory (Liberal, The Battlefords).
This is an opinion expressed not by a member of the group to which I belong, but by an influential Liberal member in the legislature of Saskatchewan.
In my opinion this house is spending a great deal of time in this debate in concentrating upon a discussion of foreign trade and foreign markets, when as a matter of fact we have a great potential consumptive market at home. Many hundreds of thousands of Canadian citizens in this dominion at the present time lack the ordinary necessities of life, without considering the amenities, and it seems to me that we should be concentrating upon improving the conditions in Canada so that we might find a larger consumptive market within this dominion at the present time. Many of our people could consume more butter and more meat, for an example, if they could buy those commodities, and to my mind this house ought to be considering ways and means of increasing that consumptive power. As hon. members realize, I believe, this cannot be done by the issue of relief, although the standards of relief should be raised; or by the issue, as our social credit friends suggest, of dividends; but I do believe that there are essential public works which could be used to build up a better Canada and at the same time distribute purchasing power so that our people could buy the commodities which at the moment we are trying in vain to export. That would give the added advantage of paying wages, instead of relief from which we get nothing at all.
Of course I realize that we must trade, because there are some things we cannot produce which we must get from abroad, and to get those things from abroad we must export something in payment of them. To-day nations are placing quotas and embargoes

against trade from without. So that whether we like it or not, some form of planned commerce between nations is in the making, and even this treaty is symptomatic of that fact. For here, written into a treaty to which Canada is a party, you have quotas for primary produce going into the United States and into Great Britain.
Now what can we do? The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman), whose speeches I always appreciate because they contain a wealth of information and of detail, would say that we have got to get free trade, or at least much freer trade. But to my mind the competitive system under which old-fashioned free trade might have flourished has gone. The competitive system both internally and externally has broken down. Internally great corporations and monopolies occupy the field of industry and of distribution, and in the world to-day both great international monopolies and self-sufficient nationalisms are being built with great rapidity.
The house has a right 'to ask what the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation would suggest in the face of this situation in regard to external trade. May I quote from our own platform and explanation of that program? We urge in the realm of external trade that we-
-set up import and export boards to encourage and regulate external trade and remove the burden of the tariff.
Let me read also our explanatory note:
Opponents of planning try to infer that this would lead to national self sufficiency. On the contrary, the more intelligent our economic relationships become, the more it will be realized that a nation, like an individual, is foolish to try to produce something expensively which can be made elsewhere more efficiently and economically. High tariffs are but walls against our income which help to build those great monopolies that oppress us. Trade ought to be an intelligent exchange of goods and services.
But the necessities of capitalist production make this impossible. For capitalism never distributes among the producers a sufficient amount of purchasing power to enable them to purchase the goods produced. Hence each nation tries to export more and more surplus goods and import less and less from abroad. High tariffs, national self-sufficiency and a struggle for the few remaining markets follow. This leads to threats of war and, finally, to war itself.
And this concluding paragraph:
The C.C.F. proposes that our international trade shall be planned intelligently so that the nation itself, through its import and export boards, shall arrange for the exchange of goods it can produce economically for those it needs and which others can produce more advantageously. Not until capitalism is banished from the earth can the ideal of universal free

trade be realized. Under a Cooperative Commonwealth policy Canada can improve its external trade, remove the burdensome tariff exactions and expand the home market. This would bring great benefits to producer and consumer alike.
That, I believe, is a fair summary of the position of this group in relation to trade and commerce; and may I say it is a realistic approach. Moreover, unless democracy plans to increase the abundance and distribute that abundance, I am afraid that the people will turn to some other form of government or to some other system. And I, believing as I do that our democratic institutions offer still the best vehicle for social and economic improvement, desire to see something done which will strengthen our democratic institutions and democratic ideals among our people. For youth, hundreds of thousands of them, and the unemployed-altogether over a million of them, on relief-will not wait; indeed they cannot wait until, even if it were possible, we could establish universal free trade or attain universal trade agreements. As I said at the outset, let us make such agreements when we can, but let us suffer no illusions that such agreements are -going to bring to o-ur people the immediate relief which is so necessary. For trade treaties are not a universal panacea, and very largely, may I say, because they are not universal; nor are -they likely to become universal. They will not cure, let me emphasize, our own immediate problems, of unemployment and of poverty. In December, I noticed, we had 407,000 persons registered as unemployed and upwards of a million individual citizens on relief; while workers' wages, another factor in the consumptive field, averaged in industry last year only 116 a week. And this, may I say to my hon. friends opposite, after many years of Liberal administration and Liberal policy.
My purpose in rising this afternoon is to ask members on all sides of the house if they do not think it is high time that this parliament and those who comprise it should face the realities of the present situation. For surely democracy is on trial. Let me repeat, unless our democratic institutions can be made to work to provide our people with opportunities of employment, with opportunities of sharing in the abundance which the resources of the country and the machinery of production make possible for us, then surely they will turn to some other form. Indeed there are threats from many quarters to-day. All across the country one can find what one might term incipient fascism as well as fascism of the blatantly European type; and then we have the growing propaganda for a so-called national government, a national government which, in my opinion, if formed, would be formed of those who desire solely to protect the vested interests in the country rather than the interests of the great masses of the people. To my mind, if these paths were followed they would simply be some more of those blind alleys up which we have been running from time to time.
There is no universal panacea that will immediately solve these problems for us. Our problems in my opinion have to be solved in the light of ultimate aims, step by step. We have got to build the path by which we shall go forward; and because I believe that this treaty is, if only a feeble step, at any rate a step in the right direction, I am supporting it on these grounds. I believe that democracy is quite capable not only of producing abundance but of distributing that abundance to the people of this country. To my mind these times constitute a challenge to every one of us and I should like to see this trade treaty disposed of as quickly as possible now that it has been discussed fairly thoroughly, so that we might proceed with the consideration of those weighty domestic problems that confront us at this moment. And so I support the treaty, though without any illusions that it is going to solve the grave problems that we face in Canada to-day.

I have
listened with a good deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who has just taken his seat. He always delivers an interesting address. He started out by stating that he was going to vote for the approval of this trade agreement, and he gave as the reason that it would promote international peace and goodwill. Well, when we come to consider the parties interested in this three-cornered arrangement, Canada, the United States and Great Britain, and take into account the harmonious and friendly relations that have existed for a long period of years, one wonders if anything can be added which will improve those relations. To me, this is just so much gilding and glitter that has been placed upon this agreement.
Then the hon. gentleman proceeds to relate a number of objections which he has to the agreement, and it appears to me they are very real and very serious ones. In fact, if I were a judge and were compelled to decide, after listening to his arguments in support of the treaty and those he advanced against it, I should have to decide that his arguments against it were very much stronger than those in favour of it.
I propose to deal briefly with two or three matters in connection with this agreement.

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
Let me refer to two statements appearing in Hansard, both made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). On page 55 you Will find the statement by the right hon. gentleman, that in dealing with this treaty we should consider the sequence of events; and in a sketchy way he reviews the events over a period of years leading up to the making of this agreement. Then there is another statement on page 56 which I desire to read, because I think it is important that we should deal with it. On page 56 the right hon. gentleman says:
May I say at once to my hon. friend that when we discuss trade matters we are almost certain to differ diametrically because wre view matters in an entirely different light. I believe the way to help to improve economic conditions, employment and the like is to encourage trade and to obtain as much in the way of trade as we possibly can. My hon. friend opposite^ believes in the policy of economic nationalism.
In considering the first of these statements as to the sequence of events, I think it is only fair to review the conditions between 1920 and 1930. Those were years of expanding world trade, years in which the trade of Canada expanded in common with the rest of the world and we enjoyed the advantages and the benefits of that world trade. We must not forget that at all times our prosperity is bound up with world prosperity and that conditions arising outside Canada influence conditions in our own country, a fact which sometimes our friends opposite seem to have overlooked in dealing with the conditions between 1930 and 1935.
At the end of 1929 and the beginning of 1930 the markets of the United States were practically closed to Canada because of the increases in the tariff on two occasions by the United States. The world depression had set in. Trade had become disorganized. There was financial chaos, exchange was dislocated, unemployment in Canada was becoming serious. It was more serious than was realized at the time; we were without accurate statistics on the subject. Following this there was dumping of manufactured goods from the United States into Canada without any reference to costs of production, with resulting disorganization of industry and increased unemployment. It is perfectly clear that something had to be done. The steps that were taken between 1930 and 1935 were, I think, the only ones that could have been taken in the circumstances.
An emergency tariff was introduced with the object of lessening unemployment and preventing this ruthless dumping of foreign products in the Canadian market. Concurrently with the raising of duties for this pur-
pose there was an understanding and agreement with the manufacturers of Canada that the prices of their products to the consumer would not be increased. That agreement was respected. There was one case where perhaps it was not, and the penalty immediately followed ; their increased protection was removed. The fulfilment of the agreement not to raise prices was strikingly exemplified in the agricultural implement industry; during all those years the prices were not raised. But following 1935, when the duties were reduced by this government, the prices of agricultural implements increased.
The objects of the emergency tariff were in a measure realized. And in dealing with this it must not be forgotten that there were many reductions in the tariff before 1935. Go back to the budget speeches and you will find a long list of items upon which tariffs were reduced over that period.
It must also be borne in mind that during that time Canada retained her share of the world's trade. There was only so much trade to be done in the world; it had shrunk by about sixty per cent.
Another step was taken in the meeting of the empire economic conference in Ottawa in 1932. I have here a report of the proceedings of that conference. I propose to read a number of extracts showing the position taken by the then prime minister of Canada and the prime minister of Great Britain.
On page 69 appears the following statement by the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, then prime minister of Canada, chairman of the conference :
What do we hope for from this conference? The answer is, I think, from all of us, greater markets within the empire. This is the answer from all of us undoubtedly, if we are persuaded, as I am, that greater empire markets mean as well greater world markets. For to us in Canada closer empire economic association does not mean in any sense world dissociation. The trading potentialities of this empire are great. But even one-quarter of the human race cannot profitably shut itself off from contact with the rest of the world.
When we reach an agreement by which our products pass more freely from one empire country to another, we drive clear channels through the stagnant pools dammed up by the world upheaval, and naturally we will carry past the boundaries of the empire and to its benefit, establish once more again throughout the world that commerce which is its very life blood. The British people in their vigour, industry, and experience have nothing to fear from foreign competition when they are united in that economic association which is now possible. When from this conference that results, we will welcome fair and friendly competition. In our own interest we will welcome it.

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
And at page 70 we find another statement:
I have said before, and I do not desire to minimize the fact, that Canada must have greater export markets for its natural products. No country can live unto itself in this complex age, and with our relatively small population, with our vast and varied natural resources, with our immense exportable surplus in natural products, we perhaps above all other countries must be assured of other markets than our own. And I confidently believe that the people of the United Kingdom will not hesitate to support our proposal, knowing on their part that it will mean increased prosperity to many of their basic industries, and through them increased prosperity to all classes in the land.
Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin, prime minister of Great Britain, speaking on the same occasion, said, as reported on page 72:
Looking at the situation from another aspect, the trend to-day is towards larger units. International trade is so hampered by barriers of all kinds that a strong opinion is developing in favour of groups, not necessarily political m character, but offering to members economic advantages in the mutual opening of markets. No one suggests that complete free trade within the empire is possible. Considerations of revenue and of past policy stand in the way. But equally there can be no doubt that more constant comunications and more complete information about imperial market requirements would, if properly focussed, present governments with opportunities of securing trade with other countries of the empire, and of making commercial arrangements with other groups of nations such as could hardly be reached if each government acted alone.
What then should be the first aim of this conference? It. should be to clear out the channels of trade among ourselves. For that purpose we need not measure too closely or too exactly the relative value of preferences given and received. If we all approach the problem with a view to seeing how much each can contribute to the common stock without detriment to our own national interests, we shall not need to concern ourselves with the relative advantages obtained by each, since we shall know that an increase in the purchasing power of any member of the empire must show itself m increased imperial trade, and the prosperity of each will add to the prosperity of all.
The present universal depression makes the extension and improvement of imperial trade a matter of urgent importance to all parts of the empire. The extension and greater activity of empire trade is the most hopeful means of stimulating demand in the world markets and of restoring a sound level of wholesale commodity prices.
Let us look, Mr. Speaker, at the results of that conference. Eleven agreements were negotiated-United Kingdom-Australia; United Kingdom-Union of South Africa; United Kingdom-New Zealand; United Kingdom-India; United Kingdom-Newfoundland; United Kingdom-Southern Rhodesia; United Kingdom-Canada; Canada-Irish Free State; Canada-Union of South Africa; Canada-Southern Rhodesia and Union of South Africa-Irish Free State. These agreements, all making in the
direction of expansion of trade, were opposed by the present Prime Minister and all those associated with him, with the exception of one hon. member, the member for the constituency now called Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Ilsley). In speaking the other day he said he had a very intelligent constituency. He must have. As I say, he was the only one on that side who supported that agreement. His electors were intelligent enough to realize its advantages, and now he says they are still intelligent and are prepared to recognize the reduction of the advantages. He is to be congratulated on having a constituency of that kind.
These agreements were negotiated, and I do not think any member of this house or anyone outside of it will deny that they were of great advantage to the agricultural producers of Canada and to the trade of Canada and the empire generally. Time has fully demonstrated the results.
Following that, the attitude of the United States changed. To a certain extent it softened towards Canada, fortunately, and presented us with the opportunity of expanding our trade in their direction. This opportunity was embraced by the then government, and I propose to read from the white paper to which the Prime Minister referred in his address, entitled The Trade Negotiations between Canada and the United States, 1934 and 1935, which may be found quoted in full in Hansard of 1936, at page 56. This is the letter from the Canadian minister at Washington to the Secretary of State of the United States. It is dated November 14, 1934:
Sir,-
The government of Canada for many months have been giving careful consideration to the means whereby the exchange of commodities between Canada and the United States might be increased, and I have been instructed to present a statement of their views for the information of the government of the United States. The government of Canada believe that the time has come for definite action and that the declared desire of both governments to improve conditions of trade between the two [DOT] countries should now be carried into effect by the negotiation of a comprehensive trade agreement.
You will recall that when the Prime Minister of Canada visited Washington in April, 1933, at the invitation of the president of the United States, the development of trade between the two countries was sympathetically discussed. On April 29, 1933, Mr. Roosevelt and Mr. Bennett issued a joint statement at the end of their conversations, which concluded as follows:
"We have also discussed the problems peculiar to the United States and Canada. We have agreed to begin a search for means to increase the exchange of commodities between our two countries, and thereby promote not only economic betterment on the North American continent, but also the general improvement of world conditions."

Within that period of time Canada has made trade agreements with several European countries.

In some quarters the statement has been made that these agreements render difficult the negotiations of a comprehensive and effective trade agreement between Canada and the United States. The agreements concluded at Ottawa in 1932 have been of immense importance in increasing the trade between the several nations of the British commonwealth. The market of the United Kingdom in particular has been a most valuable outlet for Canadian products. In return for the market thus assured Canada has continued and enlarged the preferences which had been accorded the United Kingdom since 1897. The Ottawa agreements do not, however, preclude and in fact have not precluded the signatories from offering extensive and valuable tariff concessions to other countries, and it may be stated positively that the government of Canada is free to enter into an agrement with the United States covering a wade range of products.

duction and a huge home market. But I think he overlooked the fact that while that was true, they also had the additional advantage of the highest protective wall of any country in the world. They had it going and coming. Our position was not as favourable in the same ratio. We had a low tariff. We applied no quotas against them, while they adopted quotas against us. We made no provision to hear the parties affected by reductions in the tariff, and we started out with an unfavourable trade balance.
We had only one small advantage, the preference in the British market. Let us look at where we stand now. Under the agreement now before the house we have to some extent lost the benefit of that preference, something which for years we made desperate efforts to obtain. We have lost some of that which we found to be of permanent value. We have an unfavourable balance of trade which is likely to be increased by further reductions of duties. The rates against many of our commodities going into the United States are higher than the rates on the same commodities coming into Canada. The reductions provided for in the United Kingdom-United States agreement will probably enable the manufacturers in the United States to export direct to the United Kingdom instead of continuing to maintain the branch factories which they established in Canada in order to take advantage of the British preference. If that occurs, there will be an increase in unemployment in industry in Canada because of the closing of plants and the increase in imports to follow.
We will lose some revenue because of the wiping out of the excise tax. Apparently it will have to be wiped out on everything. This would seem to be an inevitable consequence which possibly was not anticipated. Our railways and ports will lose traffic. We shall have an opportunity of discussing this in committee and of bringing out the advantages and disadvantages of the agreement. There are some advantages. With the necessary information before us we shall be able to arrive at conclusions, but as I see it now, with all the information that is available, the advantages in favour of the United States far outweigh any advantages or benefits to Canada by any concession under this agreement.

In rebuttal I would say that I do not think the leader of the opposition would advocate the casting of all ballots into one barrel or hat and the distributing of them pro rata throughout the country. There are some, I know, who believe in proportional representation and the single transferable vote. According, however, to the record of what has taken place in this country-I refer particularly to the provincial elections in Alberta in 1926 and 1930-the single transferable vote and proportional representation did not give any fairer, in fact, did not give as good a representation, in the provincial legislature as does the present system of plurality votes. Let me quote the figures.
In 1926, 68,896 votes were cast for the United Farmers of Alberta, and they got 42 seats; 36,692 were cast for the Liberals, who got five seats, and 26,197 were cast for Conservatives, with no seats.

The British Columbia lumber industry is extremely pleased by the conclusions that have been reached in this long-drawn-out and difficult, triangular trade agreement.
Our industry recognized all along that some sacrifices would have to be made to make it possible for the two great English-speaking nations to get closer together, and we feel that our government representatives have protected our interests in an admirable way, considering the many traders, producers and consumers who are entitled to serious consideration.

That was the statement of the president of the British Columbia Lumber and Shingle Manufacturers' Association comprising every lumber and shingle concern in that province. Then we have the statement of the past president:
J. H. McDonald of New Westminster, former president of the British Columbia Lumber and Shingle Manufacturers' Association, and a leader

in its trade extension work, welcomes the triangular agreement and thinks it must be regarded as generally satisfactory.

The agreement to do away with the necessity of marking all lumber going from Canada is one of the finest things the trade could have obtained. He also welcomes the increased United States quota for British Columbia shingles as a promise of better conditions in the shingle industry.
One of the most important factors with respect to the lumber industry is the removal of the Marking Act. I wonder how many members realize the significance of this to the lumber industry of British Columbia. If the Marking Act of the United States passed against Canadian lumber last year had been kept in effect, it would have meant that no Canadian lumber would have been sold in Washington. Oregon and other states. Not only so, but even lumber that might have entered that market would have gone in at a greatly added cost to the lumber manufacturer. Consider, first of all, the shipment of mouldings, fine small lumber for house interiors. Those exporting that would have to employ extra, labour to stamp every single piece, and it was estimated that this would cost at least $20 a carload extra for this class of lumber. Apart from that, I doubt whether, if that requirement had been imposed, we would have sold any lumber in the United States.
We are aware of the intense nationalism prevailing in some quarters in the United States, which are demanding that the American people use nothing but United States lumber and other articles. If an agitation of that kind were set going in the United States, what trade unions or other bodies would have been willing to use lumber stamped as Canadian lumber? In passing, might I place on record some figures regarding shipments of lumber to the United States. I want, however, to be fair; no one would deny that the British market is of some importance to us. Action must be swift and direct to produce that expansion of food production from our own soil which I think is necessary. I know of no more important task than of ensuring that in all circumstances there should be adequate supplies of food for our population in times of emergency.

Mr. Speaker, the only issue in this debate is whether this is a good trade treaty or not. We are not discussing whether a trade treaty between Canada and the United States or between the United States and Great Britain should have been negotiated. Those treaties have already been made. On this side of the house we evidently believe that this is a good trade treaty. The opposition, however, seem to think.it is not. I believe that reasonable people will agree with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) when he says that time, and time alone, will tell.
Even as a doctor, I would not care to predict the sex of a child before it was bom, and I am sure that the leader of the opposition would not, but there are certain things I can predict from heredity. I can be certain, if a child is the offspring of certain lines of white people, it will be white, but I cannot tell what its actions will be when it grows up. Some of its actions may be good and some of its actions may be bad. That is the old Mendelian theory.
The heredity of this child is good. I like its colour, and I think we should give it a chance to prove its usefulness before we judge its character. Because of the eugenics of the mating I have high hopes for this child.
There is a story told of an astrologer who had offended one of the great French kings, and who was about to be beheaded. The French king called him and asked him to predict the date of his death upon the guillotine. The astrologer replied, "Four days before your majesty's death." Needless to say he still kept his head.
The opposition seems to be forecasting a somewhat similar fate for his majesty's Canadian government. Unfortunately in the past we have done something to justify this prediction. We tried to strike a death blow at Toryism by providing for a reduction in tariffs, and about four months afterwards we were "guillotined" from power. Sir Wilfrid Laurier negotiated a trade treaty, and the people did not have an opportunity to find out whether it was good or bad before there was an election. Oh, that is a long time ago. In my opinion this is a good treaty, and I am so sincere in that belief that I want to see it proved. Should an appeal be made to the people of Canada to return us to power on the prediction that what we have done will prove to be right, or should we appeal to them when we can point to the results of the treaty? What would have been the effects of the reciprocity treaty that was fought so bitterly in 1911, no one can say with surety. I do not intend to thresh old straw over again, but the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) the other night went back to "No truck or trade with the Yankees". He said we were at the parting of the ways; though he may not have used these words, he implied that Canada would become nine states of the American union; that annexation was in sight, and he brought forward again all the bugbears that we heard in the election cry of 1911.
I remember as a young man attending college at Kingston, and the first public meeting I ever went to was in 1911. During that year we had debates at college on the reciprocity issue and we wrote essays on reciprocal trade treaties. We thought they were a splendid thing. In fact, in the junior matriculation examinations of 1911 one of the questions on the paper was to write an essay on reciprocity. About that particular time there came to the city of Kingston a man known then as the Hon. Mr. Foster, who was heralded to speak on reciprocity. As I remember, a number of us from high school attended that meeting. We were standing at the back of the hall, and I recall vividly-because he was a splendid orator-that with all his oratorical skill, pointing to the end of the hall, he said: "Young men, this may be the first vote that you will cast; but before you
do anything, before you act on anything I may say, I would ask you to go to-morrow morning to Macdonald park and there gaze upon the statue of the great Sir John A. Macdonald. For forty years he represented this historic city of Kingston. Read on that monument the inscription: 'As for myself alone, my course is clear. A British subject I was born, a British subject I will die.' "
Well, Mr. Speaker, we wondered what he meant. We wondered whether he implied some test of our loyalty and devotion to king and country. At any rate that was the impression which was left by this great orator who spoke to us on reciprocity. The same old straw is being threshed over now, and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is trying to live over again those old, unhappy, far-off days, and those battles of long ago. He was trying a few nights ago to fight them over. In his old age he has become so vicious and so venomous. Look how venomous he has become against the Prime Minister of the country, how venomous he became a few days ago against the Minister of National Defence.
One of the chief cries of the Tories has always been that we are severing our ties with the mother country; but now, with the present trade arrangement, I do not see how they can say very much about this, because the mother country has also made a trade treaty with the United States. For many reasons it is a brimming measure of satisfaction to us to know that Great Britain has found a basis of economic cooperation with our great neighbouring republic, that great democracy to the south of us. In spite of the tendency of the leader of the opposition to scoff, I believe that this is one of the longest steps toward world stability and peace since the great war. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition was scornful of the idea that this trade agreement would promote better relations or that (ariff barriers had in any way interfered with our friendly relationship or with our mutual prosperity. He said we had had friendly relations with the great United States of America since 1812. I am sorry that he is not in his seat at the present moment, but I should like to draw his attention to those unhappy days from 1866 to 1870. That is one period in Canadian history which he evidently missed.	[DOT]
Let me quote from the hon. gentleman's book, his literary masterpiece, Life is an Adventure. In that book the leader of the opposition says at page 266:
Conditions generally were somewhat depressed through 1924 and 1925, and the tariff question became a very prominent one in the discussions in and out of parliament. The United States rather short-sightedly kept raising its tariffs

It was an exceedingly unwise attitude on the part of the American people, as Canada was their best customer among all the trading nations, purchasing annually from them hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of goods, yet year by year facing the antagonistic actions of American protectionists who forced through congress bill after bill prohibiting the import of Canadian farm products. It was the beginning of that economic nationalism which has since grown to such ridiculous proportions all over the world that world trade has been almost completely strangled. But in 1924 and 1925 it particularly affected the relations between Canada and the United States, giving rise to exceedingly antagonistic feelings on the part of the Canadians toward their neighbours. _
No more effective answer could be given to what the hon. leader of the opposition now tries to make us believe he believes. This is widely different from the view he expressed in this house when he spoke on this trade treaty. I am inclined to favour the opinion expressed in his literary masterpiece, Life is an Adventure, because at that time he did not have his weather eye on the election winds.
Tariffs-tariffs-tariffs-we have argued them until the subject is threadbare. Soon we shall have to discard this political cloak and strike out in some other direction. Yet give a man a little independence and the truth will out. "Economic nationalism which has since grown to such ridiculous proportions all over the world that world trade has been almost completely strangled." So said my authority, that distinguished soldier, parliamentarian and author, the leader of the opposition.
What is the actual tariff situation in relation to Canada? When Sir Wilfrid Laurier came into power in 1896, the average ad valorem rate on dutiable imports was, in round figures, 30 per cent. It was gradually reduced until in 1911 it was 25-9 per cent. Reciprocity would have cut this in half. After 1911 it began to mount again, although there was a considerable drop in 1917 under union government. When the Liberals came into power in 1921, it again dropped and remained fairly constant until the Tories came into power in 1930. Then up it went sky-high. Since the present government came into power, it has gradually declined. But the point is that over a protracted period we have drastically reduced tariffs. In fact, in 1938 the ad valorem duty averaged 23-9 per cent, compared with 23-8 per cent in 1917. The point I wish to make is that the Liberal party worked for three or four or five years in
{Mr. Fleming.]
order to get the tariff down to where it was when they went out of power, and then when we go to the country and tell the people that we have reduced the tariff, is it any wonder that even if they do not think we are deliberate prevaricators, at least they think we are a little careless about the truth? We work and get the tariff down but by the time we have it back to where it was when we left office the people do not realize what we had to do.
There are certain things omitted from this tariff cut that I should like to have seen in it. I was pleased this afternoon to hear the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell); what he said seemed to me real Liberalism. That is the Liberalism we should be preaching in western Canada. I have continually stressed the fact that prices of farm implements and gasoline are far too high, and I see no mention of them in the trade treaty. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who is not in his seat to-night, has told us that there are international combines and that we should smash them. Well, I say to the government that if we cannot smash those international combines and reduce prices of farm implements and the price of gasoline, the government may possibly be smashed. Some way must be found to deal with these problems.
I was pleased to hear the other day the answer to a question as to certain agreements that we have in connection with our trade relations with Germany. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Usley) told us that we have certain trade treaties. Since that time I have discussed the matter with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler), and I find that on October 22, 1936, a provisional trade agreement was made between Canada and Germany, and that we have increased our sales of goods to Germany from $3,000,000 in 1936 to $18,000,000 in 1938.
How individual items will work out, no one can tell, but I trust that the results of the treaty will be beneficial to the Canadian people. As to the principles underlying this treaty I have every confidence that it is as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said this afternoon, a step in the right direction. I hope and wish and pray that it will develop into a dog-trot race to prosperity.
At the present time we are faced with an armament race. If the situation could be boiled down to a single reason, that reason is antagonisms aroused by protective systems, national isolationism, economic self-sufficiency, resulting in international hatreds. Nations have entrenched themselves in tariff dug-outs and thrown round themselves a wall of

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
bristling steel. On the other hand, freer commercial intercourse promotes mutual knowledge and trust. I was glad to hear the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other day state that when he went to the League of Nations and they sat round a common council table and got better acquainted with one another, they were able to discuss their problems in a much more satisfactory way.
All the world contributes to our breakfast table, to our comforts and the convenience and fullness of our lives. Civilization is based upon cooperation; if we refuse to do our part in this wholesome development, this natural way of living, we are contributing to darkness and distrust, and fundamentally are not only anti-social, but anti-Canadian. Our opponents base their arguments on self-interest, or protection. The only logical conclusion is that if we are not going to trade with others, we trade with ourselves only. I can do no better than adopt the language used by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) some time ago when he said that the channels of trade can be deepened and broadened only by deepening and widening the channels of goodwill.
Canada is a country which recognizes that her destiny as a great nation is to be fulfilled not behind impenetrable tariff walls, which not only shut in but shut out, but rather under a policy that will remove tariff barriers, unfetter trade and provide reasonable facilities for the inflow and outflow of goods and for the dispersal over the seven seas of the surplus which providence has so unstintingly bestowed upon us. Would they have us destroy our position as the fifth trading nation of the world? Would they have us use only such things as are indigenous to or produced in Canada? Carry their argument to its ultimate conclusion and you see what a muddle and mess we should get into. We do not want war; we do not want economic conflict; we want a decent chance to produce the things we can produce and exchange the surplus for other goods. If I am a wheat farmer I am not obliged to believe that I must eat only bread and wear a skirt made of straw in order to enjoy an economic utopia. We can participate in economic appeasement without its indicating a back-stroke against self-government or domestic economic advancement. Indeed, internationalism on one hand and national self-government on the other are the very essence of democracy.
Even if the Tories did succeed in their object of excluding foreign goods which would compete with our domestic production; even if we achieved complete control of our domestic market, there is no reason to believe that
this would increase distribution so that the Canadian people could enjoy the full output of Canadian industry. In fact, all the experience we have had of such a situation, when isolationism was throttling trade, showed that this pious hope was doomed to complete disillusionment. As a matter of fact, a few years ago we called it depression. Let me ask these questions: Was Canada less able to produce in the depression period? Had our domestic customers disappeared? Had Canada's resources in some inexplicable way become depleted? Was there no man power available? Had somebody destroyed our factories? If our domestic market is the economic paradise, why did we not simply exploit it and grow fat?
Someone will promptly say: "Oh. well, we did not have any money." I am not going to enter now into any monetary argument because I understood the Minister of Finance to say that there was a proper time and place for that, and that was when the barons of the Bank of Canada would appear before the banking and commerce committee. But if you conceive of money as gold, we are as rich as almost any nation in the world. If you conceive of it in terms of goods and services, we have the physical ability to produce the goods and the people willing to furnish the services.
Almost since time immemorial the two great parties in this country have 'been arguing tariffs, and evidently there is something to be said on both sides or the argument would not have continued so long. I am not one of those who believe that my opponents are complete fools. But the great difficulty that I see is that tariffs give primary benefit, and, in many instances, the sole benefit, to the big interests. The tariff has become a tax which differentiates between the masses and the classes. I say this because I believe we cannot struggle along indefinitely on a system predicated on benefit to the few. I cannot see the masses suffering forever the sight of the goods they need being destroyed so that a few people may grow rich in money power.
What will be the solution? As the leader of the opposition said, time, and time alone, will tell. But as a member coming from the wind swept prairies of western Canada, I say to the Liberal government sitting here for the fourth session of this parliament, that if they do not do something for the people of western Canada by reducing the price of farm implements and the price of gasoline and increasing the price of primary products, there will be such a revolt when the government goes to the country-

Mr. Speaker, someone has likened this trade agreement to a horse trade. We have made the trade, but we have not got our horses home yet.
The last speaker (Mr. Fleming) has said that time will tell. There was such a lot of ballyhoo attached to the launching of this trade treaty that people are now beginning to think that it is not what it was represented to be. But; now they are told-have patience -it is going to take time to work it out. We were told the same thing in 1935, what great benefits were going to come from the treaty of that year, and how expanding trade was going to solve all our problems. According to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), at that time it was going to solve our great problem of unemployment, stimulate industry, and give more business to our railways, which would be in a much better position because of the trade treaty. But we find, on looking over the country, we have unemployment just as bad as ever, we still have our railway deficits with us, and our industries still languish. I wish that some hon. member opposite, before this debate is concluded, would tell us exactly what benefits we have derived from the treaty of 1935. We know pretty well how it has worked out. Apparently it failed to put people to work, nor did it create any more business for our railways. According to trade returns which have been put on Hansard during this debate, the United States is the party that has benefited most from that treaty. Canadian industries have not flourished because of it; in fact, many of them are in a worse position than in 1935.
This trade treaty differs in that it is a triangular arrangement. The Prime Minister, for political effect, has represented this triangular trade arrangement as an international peace move signifying especially a rapprochement between Great Britain and the United States. This has tended to ward off criticism or even examination of the actual terms of the trade bargain. But I think the impression which the Prime Minister sought to give was exploded by my leader (Mr. Manion), who referred to denials from both London and Washington that the trade deal had any relation whatsoever to international politics. It was considered by Washington and London as entirely an economic bargain, and I think that is how we should look at it in this country. It is not a political bargain but an economic bargain entirely, and as Canadians we must consider it from that point of view.
The discussion of this matter, to my mind, involves two questions: First, is it desirable

to have freer trade relations with the United States? Second, are the terms of the agreement as a whole beneficial to Canada?
On the first point, the desire for freer trade relations with our neighbours to the south, I think I can safely say that we are all in absolute accord.
As to the second we are not in accord. The Prime Minister and his followers apparently regard the terms of this trade agreement as highly satisfactory; but many of us on this side of the house, after having given the agreement careful study, believe that, on the whole, while this or that particular item might be beneficial to us, it is not in the best interests of Canada.
My first criticism is the same as was directed against the trade treaty of 1935, against quotas being applied to this country. We have given to the United States, a country of 125000,000 people, everything we had to give, without any restrictions as to quotas. But they are not prepared to give this country the same treatment. Surely it cannot be considered an even deal if we, with a population of 11,000.000 people, must accept quota restrictions on many items of vital concern to us. There is a quota against our shingles, a quota against our cattle, a quota on cream, a quota on milk, and a quota on potatoes. We find we are under a handicap from the very beginning, therefore, in making a fair trade arrangement with the United States.
As has already been pointed out in this debate, the maximum tariff reduction which the president is authorized to make of his own initiative was 50 per cent of the existing rate. The United States tariff is a Republican tariff, the highest tariff in the history of the United States, and even with a 50 per cent reduction it is higher than the Underwood tariff, under w'hich we had free entry into the markets of the United States for a large number of our products.
Second, the powers of the president were restricted as to the duration of the agreement; it was limited to a three-year term.
But the United States did not stop there. They declared, further, that before any bargain of any kind was made with any other country it was essential that the citizens of the United States should be accorded an opportunity of appearing before a tariff board. They had the privilege of filing briefs or presenting arguments concerning any proposal. No such opportunity was given the people of this country. The people of the United States had that advantage over us.
In my opinion this trade arrangement will be most harmful to many Canadian producers. But then the Prime Minister reminded us that the consumer is to benefit. He recited a

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
long list of benefits that would accrue to the consumer; fresh fruit and vegetables, canned vegetables, many types of fish, whisky, cigarettes, and some lines of clothing would come in at reduced rates. What benefit will this be to the consumer, if he has not the money to purchase these commodities, or if he has not a job? That is the question we must consider.
Naturally the next question is: What is the price we are going to pay? What concessions are we called upon to make? That is the question we must ask ourselves at this time. We are giving up some valuable British preferences, preferences we had in the greatest market of the world. We are giving up much of the practical advantage of the Ottawa agreements. British Columbia is one province that knows the value of those agreements. The 10 per cent preference on lumber gave our province a tremendous market in the old land. Our apple growers know the value of the dollar per hundredweight on Canadian apples. Then, we had the wheat preferences, valuable in itself, and especially valuable in the development of Canadian ports.
We are sharing the preference on fruit and lumber, and we are giving up the wheat preference. The United States apparently considers these concessions of real value to them. Let me quote from comments respecting the United States-United Kingdom agreement, as issued from the Department of Commerce at Washington. This is the United States viewpoint, in regard to grains:
One of the most important concessions is the removal of the duty on wheat, which has been equivalent to about six cents per bushel. This has tended to divert trade to Canada and Australia. The United States formerly sold great quantities of wheat to the United Kingdom and with normal crops in the future and the restoration of free entry it should again be able to sell large quantities. Also-
Listen to this-
-as a removal of the preference, it should be possible for American ports and transportation interests to regain their lost business in the transhipment of Canadian wheat to the United Kingdom.
Take the business away from Canadian ports. Then, in regard to fruit, this is the United States viewpoint:
The United Kingdom has long been the most important foreign outlet for American apples. Formerly this country-
The United States.
-was the dominant supplier of British imports, but since 1932 duty margins against American apples have shifted some of the trade to British empire countries which enjoy free entry; the duty is reduced by one-third by the agreement. This concession should help the American apple export trade to regain a substantial portion of 71492-80S
its share of the British market displaced through the former duty.
Those preferences were real. They meant markets for Canadian producers. They meant employment for Canadians. They meant dollars in the pockets of Canadians, and purchasing power flowing through Canadian business houses.
What are we getting in return? We are told we are getting some concessions in the United States market for our lumber, regarded by some of some importance, but with which I shall deal a little later on. We are to get concessions for some of our cattle, some of our milk, some of our cream and some of our potatoes. In introducing the resolution the other day the Prime Minister made the following statement:
British Columbia will be greatly benefited by the concessions with respect to forest products.
Let me say that those of us coming from British Columbia are most anxious that the timber industry of our province should be benefited, not injured, by the agreement. I can safely say the timber industry in our province is our most valuable industry. Under normal conditions we have two hundred mills operating, representing a total investment of close to $100,000,000. The whole economic life of British Columbia is bound up in the welfare of the timber industry. When the lumber markets are active, general prosperity prevails. Depressed conditions are usually traceable to a slump in forest products. It is estimated that at least 75 per cent of the business in the coastal area of the province depends basically on the revenue derived from wood and its derivatives.
The empire agreements, so bitterly opposed by hon. members opposite, have been the most important single contribution to the development of off-shore business during the past seven years. The United Kingdom, which bought less than 100,000,000 feet a year prior to the trade agreement, has in recent years been absorbing more than 600,000,000 feet. The total water-borne exports to different parts of the empire have crossed the billion dollar mark. Unfortunately 1938 has not been such a happy year for the industry. It is true there was a greater shipment of lumber to the United Kingdom; yet the returns were not commensurate with the cost of production, with the result that the year was one of the worst the industry has ever had. And this is one time where under the agreement I should think something should be done-and was expected to be done-to improve this industry. [DOT]

What our lumber industry Wants to-day in addition to water-borne traffic, is a better rail market-all of which would be possible if the United States market were opened to us.
I admit, and we all agree, that the red shingle industry has been benefited by the increased quota. But in order that we may see how bright the picture is, may I refer to another wood product to which reference was made this afternoon, namely the manufacture of fir doors. The manufacture of fir doors for the United Kingdom market has developed into an extremely valuable industry in British Columbia. This industry started in 1933, as a result of preferences obtained in the United Kingdom market on account of the 10 per cent preference which was given in 1932 to empire countries. That preference was strengthened in 1935 by an increase in

At this point may I quote from a statement issued by the board of commerce at Washington. This comment, found at page 40, has reference to wood and wood products:
The duty was first imposed in March, 1932, at the rate of 10 per cent ad valorem, and was successively raised until it became 2s. 6d. per door (or 20 per cent whichever is the greater) at the beginning of February, 1935. These successive increases, which were intended primarily as a protection for the domestic door manufacturing industry, have had the effect of practically eliminating importation from the United States and diverting this trade to Canada.
The United States managed to maintain its trade with the United Kingdom fairly well through 1934, but with the final duty increased to 2s. 6d. per door early in 1935, and the building up of the industry in Canada (imports from which continued to be free of,duty) the American trade declined precipitously, until in the first half of 1938 the United Kingdom imported only 1.950 American doors, valued at about $3,500. representing only one-fifth of one per cent by both quantity and value, of the total British door imports. Conversely, imports of Canadian doors have risen from one-fifth of one per cent of the total, by number, in 1932 to 80 per cent of the total in the first half of 1938. The actual number imported from Canada rose to a high of 1,771,251 in 1936, and has since declined somewhat, but the Canadian share of the British market lias continued to increase, the imports from Canada having declined less, quantitatively, in 1937 and 1938 than the total imports from all countries.
The curtailing of and the sacrifices made by that industry will mean so many more people out of work. We cannot expect anything else when the preference is handed over. Briefly, these are the wonderful concessions to the forest products industry of which the Prime Minister boasted.
Now I ask: What about the farmer? What is there in tl is trade arrangement that will help the agricultural industry, an industry that has been struggling under depressed conditions for the last few years? Will it relieve the butter situation in Canada? Will it move the 15.000.000 pounds of surplus butter? Not a chance. Even more incredulous were the lumber operators. They were a downcast lot of men up to the day the new agreement was published. They would not believe anything could be done for them. The marking regulation is rescinded, and to top it all the quotas on British Columbia 6t and hemlock are extended, also the valuable quota on red cedar shingles is enlarged, so night has become a sunny day for the lumber people whose exports have become a big factor in Canada's external trade.
I should like to read one paragraph from a letter of Mr. W. B. Greeley, secretary-manager of the West Coast Lumbermen's Association, dated at Seattle, November 19, 1938:

Being within easy access of the large markets in Boston, New York and other large United States centres, and being able to produce finest quality potatoes at less cost than our Aroostook county neighbours, we shall be able to compete with them successfully in these large markets. I am also convinced that if the farmers of Victoria-Carleton had their choice, whether to accept the 1935 agreement or the one of 1938, they would unhesitatingly choose the present one, and I, as their representative, propose to vote for the adoption of the resolution.
