Mr. Speaker, earlier this evening we heard from the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Fleming), a fellow-member from Saskatchewan. I was interested in listening to him because I ex-
1264	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
pected he would try to point out how this treaty would benefit his constituency and the electors whom he represents. But he did not offer one really constructive argument in favour of the treaty. He indulged in flights of oratory, and I wish to congratulate him upon his ability in that respect. Then he told us one or two things. He referred to this treaty as a baby born unto this government. I think possibly it had two parents, one of them being the United States government and the other this government, but which was father and which was mother I do not care. But the hon. member, being a doctor, might have told us. Speaking figuratively, in medical terms. I would say that this baby was conceived in iniquity, born in depression, and that it will die in disgrace of its parents.
One other thing the hon. member told us, and that was that he does not want an election this year. Then in one of his flights of oratory he threatened this government that if they did not smash the implement combine^-I suppose he was referring to the combine in prices-the people would smash this government. I would ask him to recall the bold statement that was made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) during last session, I think it was, in which he threatened the implement companies as to what would happen if they did not do such and such a thing. But nothing happened. Now we have the threat of the hon. member for Humboldt to-night. I might tell the house that following the threats of the Minister of Agriculture against the implement industry, the province of Saskatchewan has now inaugurated an inquiry similar to those which took place in this house in 1937 and 1938. They have the same counsel, and I trust they will get more out of that inquiry than we did in this parliament. The whole speech of the hon. member was an admission of failure on the part of this government.
This trade agreement, Mr. Speaker, is far-reaching in its effects. It may change the whole fiscal policy of Canada, and it should be very carefully considered from the point of view of how it will affect the whole of Canada.
But first I should like to recall that the 1935 trade treaty with the United States was made after the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) had paid a visit to Washington and stayed overnight with President Roosevelt, after which he returned and the agreement was signed. But that treaty did not improve conditions in Canada, as we had been led, during the discussion in the house, to believe it would. If one reviews the trade figures of exports and imports for the first
(Mr. Perley.)
ten months of last year, compared with the corresponding months of 1937, one will find that there was a decrease in both exports and imports, and we were heading for an adverse trade balance, which would be detrimental to this country. That treaty did not do what we had been led to expect it would.
The present treaty has been conceived a little differently. The Prime Minister has told us that negotiations were carried on from February last to November 17 last, when the treaty was signed. I asked, what was the cause of the delay? I am credibly informed that the delegates from the United Kingdom and from Canada had to wait for weeks at a time, while the United States delegates consulted with representatives of American industry of all kinds whose business was likely to be affected by the agreements. Why was not Canadian industry consulted in the same manner and given the same consideration? I would ask this government to explain why the live stock industry of Canada was not consulted and given an apportunity of saying whether it was in favour of Mexico enjoying a portion of the quota we have on cattle. Why were not the wheat growers of western Canada, and the pools and the grain exchange consulted with respect to our six cent preference on wheat in the British market? I think that would have been only fair.
The Prime Minister dealt at great length, in introducing this resolution, on the gesture of goodwill that the treaty implied, and the good effect it would have on peace, harmony and unity. But I know, Mr. Speaker, what is in the minds of the western producers, and when they come to consider this treaty from that point of view they will look upon that argument as just so much eyewash. I believe the west is the hardest hit, if I may use that term, of any part of Canada by this agreement. When we have had good relations with the United States for the last forty or fifty years, or more, to suggest that now, after we have made many concessions to the United States, there will be any more harmony or unity between our two countries-well, I do not think the farmer of western Canada will swallow that.
I desire to consider this trade agreement, first, from the point of view of the price we pay for the proposed wider markets we are to have, and, second, from the point of view of how it will affect our domestic market.
Let me say at the outset that naturally a great majority of the people in the west are inclined to favour lower tariffs, and would receive with pleasure any reduction which would mean a lower price on the goods we have to purchase. But I believe the western

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
producer is fair to the extent that he does not desire any benefit at the expense of his fellow Canadian. That is the way in which we are prepared to view the question. I believe in these matters of trade and commerce, and industry, we in western Canada are fairer than we are given credit for. That, however, is the way we feel at this time.
In the past three years we have had some experience in Ihese tariff matters. For instance, we know that during the Bennett regime the duty on implements was increased. It will be recalled that a deal was made with the manufacturers* They signed on the dotted line that they would not increase the price if they got protection, and we saw lower prices. But when this government took office, two reductions in tariffs took place, reducing the rate from 25 per cent to 7J per cent, and we have seen three major increases in prices. The proof of the pudding is in the eating.
When the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) speaks-and he is the only free trader in the house, I believe-he always keeps away from any article of vital importance. He does not refer to those articles in every-day and practical use in western Canada. His reference the other night to dates was so ridiculous that it was not funny. Certainly no great importance could be attached to the comparisons he made respecting items which would affect our trade.
When introducing the resolution, the Prime Minister referred to concessions which would be of benefit to western Canada. He said that concessions affecting the prairies were received on cattle, swine, poultry, fish, lumber and feed. Saskatchewan produces only a small quantity of lumber, but may I say that there is a concession respecting white spruce which I am pleased to see. It may help that industry in the northern parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta. We may be a little selfish, but we know the effect may be that of increasing the price to the farmer who is to-day in a position to make repairs to his buildings, or to build new ones. In certain parts of the province buildings are in a bad state of repair. If the cost of repairing is increased, the change will, of course, not be received favourably.
May I say a word with respect to fish. The fishing industry can be developed in Saskatchewan. There are fresh water lakes teeming with fish in the northern part of the province. I am informed, in a letter I received the other day, that at the present time thousands of pounds of fish are piled up on the shores, and there is no outlet for the catch. I suggest that the government would do well to take this matter into consideration and to see that some outlet is provided, even if the federal government has to go to the extent of taking up the matter with the provincial government. The- fishermen are in straitened circumstances.
The treaty may offer some benefits to the poultry producers; I shall not take time to go into that matter. I regret, however, that we are losing our position in the British market. I recall that in 1932 a trial shipment from Saskatchewan, or one which was made up principally from that province, was received faiourably on the British market.
I should have liked to see that market developed.
It is scarcely necessary for me to repeat some of the arguments which have already been made with respect to cattle. The agreement is not satisfactory in its manner of operation in this connection. The fact that Mexico shares in the quota makes the whole market very uncertain.

The price was down from one and a half to two cents, and he lost about $500 on the car of cattle. Certainly that man will not forget what the quota has meant to the cattle industry. If I had time I could place on record letters I have received from other shippers who had been advised to withhold their cattle because the quota had been filled.
The duty is now at three cents, and will remain there until April 1, at which time there will be a further opportunity to fill the quota. No doubt at that time there will be a rush from both Mexico and Canada. There can be no doubt that we were not properly informed with respect to that part of the agreement. I would say further that in connection with cattle the Minister of Agriculture should direct his attention to the cattle industry in Saskatchewan. In 1937-38, as a

result of the policy adopted by the government in providing relief feed and fodder for cattle, we were dealt a blow. I shall try to deal with three or four matters in particular which affect the people in the west, and shall leave other matters in connection with industry to hon. members from eastern Canada. Under the 1932 agreements we enjoyed a preference of six cents in the British market. That was a preference in a sheltered market of 40,000,000 people. It is claimed by some hon. members supporting the government that this preference was never of any great value to us. On that point, however, I prefer to take the views of United States authorities who, after consultation with their growers, saw fit, the day following the signing of the agreement, to issue this press release:
Wheat: The granting of duty-free treatment for wheat by the United Kingdom should prove of marked value to American -wheat growers and the American wheat export trade. The import duty on non-empire wheat has been at the rate of 2 shillings per 480 pounds since November 17, 1932. A duty of this size (about six cents per bushel) applicable to wheat from some countries and not others often is sufficient to divert the trade. . . .
The United Kingdom is the leading wheat import market of the world. Formerly about a fourth of the total American wheat exports were regularly shipped to the United Kingdom. Under the influence of the world economic depression and the establishment of an import duty in 1932 (with empire wheat remaining duty-free), imports of American wheat into the United Kingdom dropped from 39,267,000 bushels in 1930 (20 T per cent of total wheat imports) to only 9.000 bushels in 1933 (less than 0-05 per cent of the total), while imports [Mr. Perley.l
from empire sources for the corresponding years rose from 79,234,000 bushels (40-5 per cent of total wheat imports) to 140,459,000 bushels (67-0 per cent of the total).
Owing to the droughts of 1934 and 1936, the United States was not in a position to supply its normal share of the United Kingdom wheat market requirements, even had there been no tariff on American wheat. In 1937, however, with a normal wheat crop, the United States supplied 6,485,000 bushels of wheat to the United Kingdom, representing 3-6 per cent of total wheat imports of the United Kingdom for that year. In view of the large wheat surplus this year in the United States and the probability that the United States will continue to be on a wheat export basis in the future, the removal of the competitive disadvantage which confronted our wheat in the United Kingdom should facilitate recovery of a larger share of that market.

The reduction to 5s. (a reduction of one-third) from the present duty of 7s. 6d. per hundredweight on these products should help to restore a substantial part of the former American share in the United Kingdom market for oatmeal.

In order to show the seriousness of the present situation, I should like to recite what I consider to be a most amazing situation with respect to wheat. We are in a period at the present time as regards marketing and prices which is comparable with only one other period since world markets for wheat came into being. The period I refer to is the three years from 1930 to 1933. I am not going to take time to quote all the figures in this connection, which I have from the statistics issued by the Food Research Institute of the United States, but I will abbreviate them a little. Well, it is a good job we had the luck. The Minister of Agriculture, speaking the other night, I think on the address, stated that the foregoing of the preference that we enjoyed had nothing to do with the diversion of wheat from Canadian ports to United States ports. I would prefer to take the opinion of the United States state department as given in a press release. I shall quote briefly what they said with respect to shipments through Canadian and United States ports.
The concession of free entry for American wheat should benefit also the American transportation and port business. In order to obtain the benefits of the United Kingdom preference, Canadian wheat, which formerly moved in large quantities through American ports has under the preference been shipped principally to the United Kingdom direct from Canadian ports. In view of this concession, American port and transportation interests will be in a position to reenter the transshipment business.
Again I prefer to take that statement as to how it affects the shipments.
I should like to recall another interesting matter. Taking a million bushels of wheat from Fort William or Port Arthur, shipping it in Canadian bottoms down the lakes through Canadian elevators, unloading and reloading, shipping it down the St. Lawrence to Canadian terminals, then on through Canadian channels to Saint John and Halifax and out to Europe-all these operations involve a cost of ten cents a bushel. It is estimated that this operation means, for Canadian shipping interests, elevator interests, payments of harbour and port fees, and labour, one hundred thousand dollars, and more than half of that is represented by labour. Consider what that means to Canadian industry, labour and shipping; consider what it means in loss to them when we forego that advantage. I

have heard over the radio, as I suppose all hon. members have, "The Shadow Knows." I say, the farmer knows and you cannot tell the farmer of western Canada that when his grain is directed through Canadian ports it does not mean something to him in the end, when 50 per cent of the cost is labour; for that means that Canadian labour will be fed with our bacon, pork and butter and cheese.

Yes, that is fine. My answer to that is this, that there are international interests in this grain business, the Big Three, which the minister should know something about. They are considered by the grain interests and the producers of western Canada to be the greatest chiselers in the market; until you eliminate them, ruination is written on the map. These men direct Canadian grain through United States ports, where they can chisel on rates, harbour fees and everything; that is what they are doing. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) could tell us a story about it if he were in the house to-night. You cannot tell the western farmer that we are not gaining anything while our grain is going through Canadian ports.
Western farmers are interested in the dairy business to quite a considerable extent. As I must hurry, I cannot take as much time as I should like to do on this phase of the agreement. The constituency of Qu'Appelle could supply about four times the amount of milk that is provided for in this quota, and it would be only one-fifth of a pint of milk and one-tenth of a pint of cream to each American once a year; that is not very much.
I am leaving to members from other parts of Canada the discussion of the effects of this treaty upon industry. They can set out their case. But from what I have learned with respect to vegetables, fruits and other commodities of that kind, I think there is very little in this agreement for us. We appreciate the fact that the main market is the domestic one. When we consider that 95 per cent of all our primary products, apart from wheat, are consumed in Canada, surely we must realize the importance of maintaining our

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
position in the domestic market. The farmers of the west realize that. They know that if they can supply foodstuffs to workmen in the
constituency of Waterloo, engaged in the manufacture of machinery for western Canada, that is better than importing products from Japan or from the south, because those workmen are eating Canadian butter, cheese, pork and so on.
The position we take in western Canada is this. We want to be fair. We do not want any advantages at the expense of any one Canadian. But I should like this government to show us-I have not been able to get it from any of the arguments that have been put forward-whereby this treaty will mean a single job more to any Canadian. The people of Canada are demanding something worth while, but the government have not shown that one young Canadian will get a job through this treaty.

There is nothing in this
treaty that will encourage any young farmer in the west to remain on the land, get married and establish a home. To my mind these treaties are dangerous. They make for competition in the marketing of some of our primary products, and while there may be a few advantages, the disadvantages materially outweigh them.
In conclusion, I should like to quote an opinion expressed by the President of the United States, who is a pretty good authority. Speaking to the American Farm Bureau at Chicago, he said:
Agriculture, far from being crucified by this agreement, as some have told you, actually gains from it. We export more agriculture products to Canada than we have imported from her. We shall continue to do so, for the very simple reason that the United States with its larger area of agricultural land, its more varied climate and its vastly greater population produces far more of most agricultural products, including animal products, vegetables and fruits, than does Canada. In the case of the few reductions that have been made, quota limitations are set on the amount that may be brought in at the lower rates.
On the other side of the picture we believe, and most unbiased men believe, that the general increase in our trade with Canada, including the exports of our factories, will so add to the purchasing power of hundreds of thousands of wage earners that they will be able to spend far more than they do to-day for the products of our own farms, our own forests and our own fisheries. Greater trade is merely another word
for more production and more employment. The proof of this particular pudding is in the eating: the best way to judge the new accord is to observe how it works out.
Mr. VITAL MALLETTE (Jacques Cartier)
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, the house is discussing to-night the resolution introduced by the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) which appears on page 8 of today's order paper, under No. 15, and reads as follows:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the trade agreement entered into at Washington on the 17th day of November.' 1938. between Canada and the United States of America, and that this house do approve of the same, subject to the legislation required in order to give effect to the provisions thereof.
As this resolution deals with the principle of the treaty rather than with the treaty itself,
I shall restrict myself to a discussion of its general principles, leaving the pleasant and interesting task of reviewing its details to the time when the treaty itself will be submitted to the house after the passing of the present resolution.
I shall be telling nothing new to my hon. colleagues when I proclaim that the Liberal doctrine, the policy of the Liberal party of Canada, has always been to seek the improvement of Canada's trade with the whole world.
Being a producing nation-more accurately, an over-producing one-we must naturally find markets for our surplus production of all kinds. The country therefore finds itself in the same position as an ordinary manufacturer who produces more goods than his regular customers can absorb. Such a manufacturer would naturally seek new markets. He would increase his advertising and extend his field of action. Therein lies the very reason for our commercial agreement with the United States.
There used to be advocates of absolute free trade, but ever since the free movement of goods from one country to another has been impeded by customs duties, quotas and restrictions of all kinds, the theory of absolute free trade has undergone substantial modification.
All Liberal administrations have been in favour of better commercial relations with the United States. They have attempted negotiations on many occasions. Those of 1910 and 1911 were on the point of working out satisfactorily for the people of Canada who believed in that sort of policy, but at the general elections of 1911, conducted by the Liberal party on the issue of reciprocity with the United States, the Nationalist opponents of the Laurier government directed a violent campaign against that government on the question of a Canadian navy. The
1272	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
Tories of the time were clever enough to take advantage of the diversion caused by the Nationalist element in the province of Quebec.
The battle-cry of the Tories throughout that election campaign was "No truck or trade with the Yankees," This slogan, which they have kept to the present day, is worth about as much as their other one-"King and chaos."
The Laurier government was not exactly overthrown on account of the opposition of the Canadian people to greater trade relations with the United States; but on account of a conjunction of circumstances which brought about the union of two different groups opposed to the Laurier government for two different reasons, a union which nevertheless resulted in the defeat of the government.
I have often heard expressions of regret about that incident which had an unfortunate effect on the commercial development of Canada. But the Tories had taken such a firm stand during the electoral campaign that they were forced, when they took power, to stick to their word and the dream of better trade relations with the United States vanished for a long time.
It goes without saying that the Canadian people wanted better relations. I could hardly find a better proof of it than the fact that the Bennett government, the most markedly Tory government which we have had for a long time, entered into negotiations with the United States to that end.
A few days before the election of 1935, I think. Right Hon. Mr. Bennett admitted that, if he were returned to power, his government would sign a trade agreement with the United States. That is proof enough of the desire of the Canadian people to broaden and tighten their trade relations with the United States.
The Bennett government had apparently done much work to that end, since the present government was able to sign the agreement with the United States just a few weeks after taking over the administration of the country.
Of course, such a view is not unanimously held by our friends of the Tory party, because quite a number of them would like to build a kind of Chinese tariff wall around Canada, a kind of magic wall which would let Canadian goods out, but would not let in goods from any other country.
That is an absolutely illogical view, because after all trade cannot be but an exchange of goods, and, although use is made of money for statistical purposes, the whole process ends in the sending of goods from one country to others and vice versa.

One of the speakers for the Tories asserted the other day his desire to maintain the standard of living of our workers. In order to achieve that purpose, he wanted to protect them from foreign competition. Well, the fiercest opponents of the present resolution would admit that the standard of living of our neighbours to the south is comparable to that of any other nation in the world. Therefore, such an argument has not much worth. Our political opponents are always speaking about protecting our producers. We share that sentiment. We wish to protect our producers in every branch and we also wish to protect the consumers in every branch, because if there is a forgotten man in the political program of the Tories it is the consumer. The Liberal doctrine, representing the happy medium, takes into account the consumer as well as the producer, for if the consumer has no money to pay for his purchases there will be nothing for the producer.
Only yesterday, one of the opposition speakers complained of the lowering of a 40 per cent duty.
Can it be, Mr. Speaker, that there are Canadian industries which cannot meet United States competition without a tariff protection of 40 per cent? Are those the industries which the Tory party wishes to protect? The people will have their say in the matter the next time they go to the polls.
It will perhaps be useful to hear what a few experts think of the new trade agreement. Speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I quoted the opinions, all favourable to the treaty, of the presidents of the Bank of Montreal, of La. Banque Cana-dienne Nationale and of La Banque Provin-ciale. Let us see now what the president of the Bank of Nova Scotia thinks of it. I quote from the Ottawa Journal of January 27, 1939:
(Text)
The importance of the new trade agreements
Canada's ability to take advantage of what further recovery may occur to the south of the border will no doubt be increased by the second Canada-United States trade agreement, which was recently concluded in Washington, together with the associated agreement between the United States and Great Britain. The Canada-United States treaty increases the concessions made by both countries under the agreement of three years ago, and is broadened to include tariff reductions on a large number of items which were not covered in the earlier arrangement. Canada secured a variety of new concessions, the most important of which were on products of the farm and of the fisheries.
There can be no doubt that the three-cornered trade agreement between the United States, Great Britain and Canada was the greatest achievement in reducing trade barriers since the onset of the depression. Unlike many

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
previous treaties, the method of giving preferential treatment through raising tariffs against other countries was not utilized. Every change in the tariff schedules of the three nations, and there were a great many of them, represented a reduction. And through the provision of most favoured nation treatment all these reductions were automatically extended to other countries. While admittedly the new arrangements have resulted in some weakening in the preferential system of the Ottawa agreements, they should do much to encourage trade between the empire and other members of the sterling "bloc" on the one hand and the United States on the other.
That is what the president of the Bank of Nova Scotia said. Then I turned to the annual report of the Dominion Bank and read with great care what the president had to say, and also the general manager. And, believe it or not, there was not a single reference to the treaty. They must be satisfied with it, or at least have no fear of it; they did not even refer to it.
Then the Banque Canadienne-Nationale- and this is something which came in just this morning-say in their monthly letter for February, 1939:
Ee nouveau traite de commerce avec la Republique voisine, qui abaisse les droits ou elargit les contingentements relatifs & un grand nombre de nos produits dont la vente est en regression, aura sur notre commerce d'exporta-tion une influence stimulante dont les effets se revelent deja.
I am inclined to think that some hon. members may not read my speech in the translation to-morrow, so I shall translate this myself right away. They say that the new commercial treaty with the neighbouring republic which lowers the customs duties and increases quotas on a large number of our products of which the sale at the moment is diminishing, will have upon our export trade a stimulating influence of which the effects are already revealing themselves.
I have quoted banks. Let us now hear what labour, the other member of the family, has to say about this treaty. This is from the memorandum presented to this government by the All-Canadian Congress of Labour on January 6, 1939, published in the January issue of the Canadian Unionist:
Canada's tariff policy.
The congress joins with the government and the people of Canada in the hope_ that the trade treaties negotiated with the United States and Great Britain will be mutually advantageous. It is recognized that any arrangements for the extension of trade between the nations involve adjustments within the nations themselves, but so long as the general welfare of the people is the primary consideration, it is felt that the producers and industries concerned should endeavour to cooperate in the effort to increase the exchange of goods and services. In its relationships with other nations, however, the congress believes that trade considerations should not be permitted to influence
the government where the fundamental issue of the maintenance of democracy may be involved.
So there you have both capital and labour in favour of this treaty. If I were to seek other backing for my argument I would quote the hon. member for London, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion). Many hon. members have quoted his book, Life is an Adventure. I do not own a copy of the book, because the price is out of reach of the proletariat, of which I am a member. But I thought I could borrow it from the parliamentary library, and on February 9 of this year I put in my request for a copy of the book. I was tofd that, although the library owns eight copies, none was available for me at the moment. I should not underline the words "for me." because there were others waiting for the book. It should please the hon. gentleman and his editor to know that at the present moment, although the parliamentary library owns eight copies of the book, there is a waiting list of hon. members wanting to get it.

There is only one more item, another argument in support of our contention which appeared in La Presse of November 19, 1938, two days after November 17, when the treaty was signed. It says:
" We may now expect our small fruits to be exported to the United States." says J. H. Lavoie, director of the provincial service of horticulture in the province of Quebec.
That is very nice coming from the government of Quebec, and there would have been many more in favour of the treaty had the government of that province entertained towards this government a more Christian attitude. But that was the only encouragement we got from that source.

A great deal of fun has been poked at the Prime Minister's use of the word "appeasement" in connection with this trade treaty; but hon. gentlemen who are not too busy might look up the Gazette, published in Montreal. a very good newspaper which has this headline on its front page in this morning's issue, "Chamberlain hopes to weld peace by trade." I admit that the old gentleman with the umbrella, may not always score one hundred per cent, but he makes a terribly good showing. Speaking at Blackburn, England, he is reported to have made this statement, which I will put on Hansard for the benefit of my Tory friends and other unbelievers :
It may well be that this approach by way of trade in which we have a common interest may turn out to be the best and quickest way of bringing about a better understanding between our two countries.
A great many statistics have been put on Hansard in this debate. I have been guilty of putting a few on myself. There is much to be said for statistics, but perhaps I may be permitted to tell a little anecdote which undoubtedly members of the house will appreciate.
A few years ago, in a moment of patriotic fervour, I joined the Montreal Canadian club. I have paid my fee every year since, and I am still a member in good standing.

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
With me it became almost a part of my religion to attend the Canadian club luncheon at the Windsor hotel, on Peel street, Montreal, nearly every Monday, the day of their weekly luncheon, and 1 remember that on one occasion the guest was Mr. Philip Kerr, who I think now adorns the House of Lords in England as Lord Lothian. At the beginning of his speech-I do not want to shock the ears of any member-he said that in his opinion there were three kinds of lies, and he enumerated them as follows: Lies, damned lies, and statistics. 1 want to say, Mr. Speaker, that those are my views too.
The King government has therefore, in negotiating a broader trade agreement with the United States, once more upheld the true interests of Canada, thereby achieving a diplomatic and commercial success for which the country will be grateful.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Euler) in the course of his remarks disposed, almost in an aside, of the importance of the concessions that are being granted by this trade treaty to thirty-eight other nations. The Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) said that the six per cent preference on wheat which Canada enjoyed in the British market is a matter of minor imp~rtance, and he also said that the lowering of the import duty on apples entering Great Britain was going to prevent the over-production of apples in Great Britain. I should like to know what we care, to any great extent at all events, about the over-production of apples there. The same argument holds good, I might say, with respect to industry in this country. The sweeping reduction under the treaties will certainly not produce over-production in a great many industries in Canada. In fact, in some places they will be closed up. It will certainly increase unemployment, and will simply mean the crucifixion of some industries.
The speeches of ministers and a great many hon. members opposite concluded with an impassioned appeal to the workers f Canada for what seems to me to be the supreme sacrifice; and all these appeals were made on the grounds of economic appeasement. In fact, so far as I can learn, no one on the government side of the house has said very much yet about employment or unemployment. This world appeasement plea has received its full share of praise. Each speaker in turn has taken a crack at the little, tiny, penny cake of soap, to put some more froth in the old hogshead.
One of the most important points is the effect of the treaty on the industrial worker. Will it give one more man in the country a
job? The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has told us that we have been requested by Great Britain to make these concessions. I do not see how the people of Canada can properly judge the merits or demerits of the treaty until they know what concessions we were asked to make. In justice to hon. members and to the country the correspondence with respect to that phase of the matter should be made public. In his statements the Prime Minister has said that we have gone no farther in making these sweeping reductions in our tariffs and in making the sacrifice of our preference in the British market than has been absolutely necessary to bring about the consummation of the treaties-at least, that is the impression he has left on the Canadian people.

my hon. friend's attention to the dispatch from the Secretary of State for the Dominions, in London, which was sent to me at Washington. in which the Secretary of State says on behalf of the British government that the agreement could not have been made except for the sacrifices that the dominions- or at least the concessions which the dominions were prepared to make in this matter.

speechtext:
I did not know that had been put on record. But the fact remains the impression has gone abroad, as I said before, that all the sacrifices and all the sweeping reductions had to be made in order that these treaties might be consummated.
I do not think the Prime Minister had any need to go farther than accede to the request of the British government with respect to what it was necessary to grant in the making of these treaties, and I feel strongly on that point. I feel, too, that ample compensation should have been given to us for any sacrifices we had to make in the British market. In this connection may I quote from the London Weekly Times of November 25, 1937:
A difficulty throughout has been that the concessions desired by the United States in the British market involve some sacrifice of the advantages hitherto enjoyed by the dominions, which, as Mr. Lyons explained on Monday in an important statement to the press, cannot be expected to acquiesce unless they can be assured of adequate compensation in other directions.
That was the principle of compensation as demonstrated by Mr. Lyons. Then the article continues:
In his statement Mr. Lyons was careful to make it plain that an Anglo-American trade agreement did not involve the surrender of the principle of imperial preference. Great Britain is not being asked to abandon her system of reciprocal preferential trade within the British commonwealth, which has had such welcome
1276	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
effects in promoting recovery in all the British countries, any more than America is being asked to abandon her system of high protection, to which, in the opinion of most Americans, she owes her unparalleled industrial development. All that is being sought is some modification in the application of these principles which, without jeopardizing any important British or American interest, will facilitate an increase in the trade between the two countries to their mutual advantage.
It is there recognized that the reciprocal preference on trade within the British commonwealth of nations has had a welcome effect in promoting recovery in all British countries, and it is pointed out that the treaty sought between Great Britain and the United States was to promote trade between those two countries. Only some modifications, without jeopardizing any interests, were needed.
The example and the results of the empire trade agreements concluded by the Conservative government in 1932 were before them. Those treaties were debated in the house for five or six weeks, and were very much maligned by the Liberal opposition of that day, which voted against them. We certainly must now give credit to the Prime Minister and to the Conservative government which held office in 1932. Those were the treaties which had such welcome effects in promoting recovery in all British countries, and which resulted in the conclusion of the United Kingdom-United States treaty of today. The United States wanted to get in on it, and they did.
What did the empire treaties mean? I quote from the London Times of November 24, 1938:
Foreign trade in the British markets not only had not suffered but had actually increased since the Ottawa conference.
And again:
Simultaneously with the Anglo-American agreement an agreement was signed between Canada and the United States revising the agreement of 1935 to meet the new situation. Other dominions did not attempt to negotiate parallel agreements, but were consulted at every turn....
The other dominions did not make parallel agreements; they did not have to. Neither did we.
What sacrifices did we make? I will mention only a few, but no doubt more and more will be found as time goes on. By losing the preference in (he British market we have shared our apple market, our wheat market, our pork market, our lard market, and the markets for several other commodities, meaning a loss of millions of dollars to our producers, our railways, our steamships and our ports. It means unem-

ployment for our producers, our railway workers, our dock workers and our sailors. The advantage to our steamships by way of preference simply meant that before a ship coming from a United States port could unload a cargo of wheat in Great Britain it had to pay $12,000. That duty has been removed and they do not need to pay it any more. A duty of six cents a bushel means $12,000 on a 6,000 ton load. There will be less incentive for our produce to be handled by Canadian railroads, Canadian steamships, Canadian elevators and Canadian ports. If the sacrifice is to be made, what compensation is being given for the sacrifice?
Apparently this sacrifice was not sufficient. The government is faking off the three per cent excise tax on the items covered by the agreement. Our industrial workers are to be sacrificed to that extent. Why did we have to reduce the tariff further on these items? Why were our vegetable growers sacrificed? Why are we to lose from $14,000,000 to $18000,000 in excise tax? We are told that this is a reduction in taxation, but there is only one way whereby you can reduce taxation- by reducing expenditures. That $18,000,000 will have to be made up in some way, Canada does not receive a single advantage for the advantages she has given. On the other hand, she shares with nineteen other nations which come under the most favoured nation clause the advantages that she has in the United States market. The London Times Weekly has this to say:
The Canadian government are being subjected to much pressure from various industrial interests to denounce the present trade treaties *with Germany and Japan, writes our Ottawa correspondent.
Even before the trade agreement -with the United States was signed the textile manufacturers in Canada were finding themselves at a serious disadvantage in coping with competition which was buttressed by export subsidies and unfair leverage of a state-controlled economic organization.
